Docker is just a container solution. You create an "image" with a Dockerfile, that defines what goes in it. The dockerfile, is used to generate a self-contained image, that includes: operating system, your code, and any other dependencies: database, cache, proxy, load balancer, etc.

You don't need to use docker, it's just that the number of old "php" webhosts have gone away. It's rare these days for anyone to want to just deploy an index.php file (ok, well not rare, just not cool anymore, nor growing in popularity).

If you want to continue to work on raw php, just choose a host that supports this: Dreamhost, Heroku, Godaddy, etc etc etc.

Docker adds portability away from any specific integration. (given that you have an orchestration configuration as well)

Yes, google cloud has all of that, however, you can still package your application into a docker image, and deploy that on google, which would then auto deploy those resources on demand. The advantage of having it in this container means you don't need to do configuration inside of google's UI, it's all defined in your image.

Now, orchestration, which is another topic, comes in multiple flavors. Docker-compose is docker's, which allows you to define these resources which can be referenced from the dockerfile.... or, you can go with kubernetes, which is google's open source alternative. Both have pros and cons, but I like kubernetes a lot.

Docker images don't "force" you to take someone else's code, they just hold the services you are used to but pre-installed into a binary image that can be run on any machine that has docker installed. The mysql docker image just has mysql server installed, you still need to link it to a directory to hold your database, and you still need to create your tables. You can download a docker image with the php interpreter and an http server already installed, but you still need to link it to your php code.

Docker automates manual sysadmin work, and the cost of learning docker is less than the cost of becoming a full sysadmin for a public web server.
